title: The Life of Master Huiyuan (Vernacular and Classical Accounts)
author: Compiled and annotated by Zhanran

inline.s: Master Huiyuan, First Patriarch of the Pure Land school, was the first to annotate that school's foremost scripture, the Buddha Speaks of the Immeasurable Life Sutra (for details see Master Huiyuan's Commentary on the Meaning of the Immeasurable Life Sutra). A Letter to the Lady Xu Fuxian). Moreover, at Donglin Monastery on Mount Lu he formed a society to recite the Buddha's name, all seeking rebirth together in the Western Pure Land. He led the assembly in diligent Buddha-recitation, had a pond dug and lotuses planted, and set twelve-petaled lotuses in the water to turn with the current, marking out the twelve double-hours of day and night as a measure for their practice. Because their principles and methods of cultivation were correct, every one of the one hundred and twenty-three members of the Lotus Society showed auspicious signs of rebirth in the Pure Land, and some, such as Liu Yimin, even saw the Buddha in this very life. This great and original collective undertaking not only verified the Pure Land Dharma gate on a large scale and proclaimed to the world that it is an incomparably supreme Dharma gate, but also opened the way for societies devoted to Buddha-recitation, exerting an immeasurably profound influence on his own time and on later ages. Sixty years later Master Tanluan (
) appeared, and close upon him Master Daochuo (
), and Master Shandao (
), whereby the Pure Land school came to its full flowering.

It must be pointed out in particular that Master Huiyuan himself not only saw the Three Saints of the West three times beforehand, but saw them once again at the very end, when Amitābha Buddha told him face to face: "In seven days you shall be born in my land." Moreover, all one hundred and twenty-three members of the Lotus Society were reborn there, each with auspicious signs. Was this not because Master Huiyuan's cultivation was of the very highest order, and because his guidance and his urging were so skillful? The profound shock this gave to his contemporaries, its promotion of the Pure Land school, and its far-reaching influence on later ages can readily be imagined; even today we can only marvel. Yet those who fly the banner of the "Pure Land school," the Primal Vow Dharma gate, scheme with all their might and use every kind of method and rhetoric to disparage and even deny Master Huiyuan, the First Patriarch of the Pure Land school! This too is a mark of the Primal Vow Dharma gate, visible everywhere in the lies and fallacies they fabricate.

[The Primal Vow Dharma gate flying the banner of the "Pure Land school"] The term "Pure Land school" originally denotes the one school among the ten schools of Buddhism that devotes itself to Buddha-recitation and seeks rebirth in the Western Pure Land, taking Master Huiyuan of the Jin dynasty as its First Patriarch,
a great school that for a thousand years has stood on a par with the Chan school

. Their so-called Primal Vow Dharma gate, however, is nothing but a small sect, yet Master Huijing brazenly takes the name "Pure Land school" for it, as though they were the whole of the Pure Land school! This is a deliberate confounding of names, passing off fish eyes as pearls and the counterfeit as the genuine, in order to deceive those ignorant of the facts, and especially beginners in Buddhism, so that they take them for the Pure Land school and board the pirate ship. This is the trick by which the Primal Vow Dharma gate lives:
Deceit!
Buddhist disciples must keep their eyes wide open:
whenever you meet a group or a website that names itself "Pure Land school," you must examine carefully whether it is in fact the Primal Vow Dharma gate, so that you are not taken in

. The way to tell them apart is quite simple. If it is led by Master Huijing, Master Jingzong, and the like, and propagates the views and theories of the Primal Vow Dharma gate, for example Pure Land School Hongyuan Monastery, Pure Land School
Pure Land School Portal
Chinese Pure Land School

Global Pure Land School Portal, the Chinese Pure Land School Association, and so forth, then it is the Primal Vow Dharma gate, an outside way that attaches itself to Buddhism, and not the true Pure Land school,
and its true names ought to be: Primal Vow Dharma Gate Hongyuan Monastery, Chinese Primal Vow Dharma Gate
Global Portal, Chinese Primal Vow Dharma Gate Association, and so on; only then would name and reality correspond

. [The ten schools] The Kosha school, the Satyasiddhi school, the Chan school, the Tiantai school, the Avatamsaka school, the Mantra school, the Dharma-characteristics school, the Pure Land school, the Vinaya school, and the Three Treatises school. [The views and theories of the Primal Vow Dharma gate] See
The Primal Vow Dharma Gate Is an Outside Way Attached to Buddhism
for details.

blocks.text: The Life of Master Huiyuan (Vernacular Account)

inline.s: The original text is taken from Records of Pure Land Saints and Sages.
Master Huiyuan (

). His secular surname was Jia, and he was a native of Loufan in Yanmen (present-day Daixian, Shanxi). Even as a child he was tireless in study, learning widely in every field and penetrating the Six Classics, and he excelled especially in Zhuangzi and Laozi. At that time Master Daoan had established a monastery on Mount Heng in the Taihang range, and Huiyuan went there to take refuge with him. When he heard Master Daoan expound the Prajna Sutra, he was suddenly and thoroughly enlightened, and he therefore shaved his head and left home to study at the feet of Master Daoan. Huiyuan was always diligent in reflection and in chanting the scriptures, advancing day and night without slackening. Daoan praised him, saying: "The one who will spread the Buddha-Dharma in the lands of the East must surely be Huiyuan
[Master Daoan (

)] An eminent monk of the Jin dynasty, a native of Fuliang in Changshan (Zhengding, Hebei), whose secular surname was Wei. The Master divided the exposition of scriptures into three sections: the introductory part, the main part, and the dissemination part, a method still in use today. He also established many monastic ceremonies, rules of conduct, and repentance rites, and fixed Shi as the surname of monks, all of which later generations have followed. His contribution to Buddhism was very great.
In the sixth year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin (

), Huiyuan passed through Xunyang and saw how broad and open Mount Lu was, a place where one might settle and dwell in peace, and so he built a retreat there called Longquan Monastery. Master Huiyong, a senior fellow disciple of Huiyuan, was already living at Xilin on Mount Lu and wished to invite Huiyuan to stay with him. But Huiyuan's fellow practitioners and his lay disciples gradually grew so numerous that Xilin was too cramped to hold them. The governor Huan Yi therefore built another monastery for Huiyuan on the eastern side of Mount Lu, and so it was called Donglin, the Eastern Grove.

Huiyuan then led the assembly in cultivating the Way of the Buddha and had a pond dug and lotuses planted. On the pond he set a twelve-petaled lotus that turned with the current, and he had the hours of day and night marked out as a measure of time, to serve as the rhythm for their walking meditation in cultivation. From then on, men of pure faith from every quarter who heard of Huiyuan's lofty conduct and integrity came to take refuge with him, one hundred and twenty-three in all.

Huiyuan said: "You gentlemen have come here to cultivate the Way; can it be that you have no thought of seeking rebirth in the Pure Land?" Thereupon they reverently made images of the Three Saints of the West, built a hall, and formed the Lotus Society, asking Liu Yimin to compose a vow text (for the full text see the Mount Lu Pure Land Collection), which was carved in stone. At that time Wang Qiaozhi and several others also composed poems on the Buddha-recitation samadhi to express their aspiration for rebirth in the Western Pure Land. Huiyuan wrote a preface for them, which reads:

What is samadhi? It is concentrated thought and stilled reflection. When thought is concentrated, one holds to the one and does not scatter; when reflection is stilled, the vital energy becomes empty and the spirit luminous. When the vital energy is empty, wisdom awakens and one can observe with clarity; when the spirit is luminous, there is no subtle or profound principle that one cannot penetrate. Concentrated thought and stilled reflection, these two, are the support of suchness: through them one can awaken into the one true dharma-realm, and from them one can give rise to the wondrous function of delivering living beings.

Yet the samadhis revealed by the Buddhas are of many kinds and many names. If we seek the one whose power is highest and whose attainment is easiest, then Buddha-recitation stands first. Why? Because one who can exhaust all inconceivable and wondrous principles and reach the most utterly still and serene, inconceivable state is honored by us with the name Tathagata. The Tathagata can both awaken into the wondrous essence of the substance and follow conditions and respond to capacities in transformation, applying himself without fixed method. Therefore he enables those who enter this Buddha-recitation samadhi to forget altogether the discriminations of ordinary knowing, and, following whatever object comes before them, to let the mind mirror it in reflection. Since the mind that mirrors all things is itself clear and pure, inner purity and outward illumination intermingle, and so all phenomena appear reflected according to the pure nature of awareness. This is not something to be reached by the ear-faculty, the eye-faculty, or other conditioned dharmas; yet the awareness of hearing and seeing ceaselessly functions in its wondrous way. Thereupon the numinous awareness reveals its aspect of serene clarity, pure and undefiled, and within the originally complete substance of pure radiance the wondrous, naturally arisen sound of Amitābha Buddha's name strikes and resonates with the perfectly illumined, pure tathagata-garbha mind. At that moment every hindrance and attachment of feeling melts away, and the suchness-nature, which is neither born nor dies, instantly shines forth. Were this not the most wondrous and supreme skillful means under heaven, how could such a state be reached?

Therefore Wang Qiaozhi and those other worthy ones who practiced according to the teaching all knew that they should cultivate this essential gateway that encompasses all Buddha-dharmas. They also felt how brief a human life is, its span of moments to be exhausted at any time, and they feared that the provisions for transcending birth and death had not yet been laid up. So they washed away the mind of discriminating delusion, settled in the hall of practice, ordered their deportment and roused their spirits, and made clear the destination of their future rebirth. At night they pressed on and forgot sleep; rising at dawn, they devoted themselves single-mindedly without slackening. Thus focusing their will on the work of cultivation, they would surely accord with the goal of the three vehicles' path of liberation within the Dharma. Above, relying on Amitābha Buddha's power to welcome and guide them, they would leap past three great asamkhyeya kalpas; and by the encouragement and mutual support of fellow practitioners they would be reborn together in the Pure Land. Below, they would guide those living beings who are timid and lacking in faith and vow, urging and encouraging them from behind so that they press forward in seeking the Pure Land. Reading the great poems on the Buddha-recitation samadhi by Wang Qiaozhi and the others in this light, how can one say that they are merely verses in which men of letters give vent to their feelings?

Because the scriptural collections in the region east of the river were greatly lacking, Huiyuan sent disciples on a long journey across the Congling ranges to obtain many Sanskrit texts and bring them into the Guanzhong region. Of all the sutras and vinaya texts of that time, nearly a hundred scrolls were circulated from Mount Lu. Huiyuan also wrote a Treatise on the Nature of Dharma, setting forth the principle that nirvāṇa is permanent. When Master Kumarajiva read it, he praised it, saying: "Though the borderlands had not yet seen the definitive Mahayana scriptures, he has nonetheless secretly accorded with the ultimate meaning of the Dharma."
[Borderlands] refers to the Chinese lands of that time, for the Dharma had come but recently and many important scriptures had not yet been translated, especially the definitive Mahayana sutras.

Master Huiyuan lived on Mount Lu for thirty years, never once setting foot in the worldly realm. Single-mindedly he cultivated the Pure Land, stilling his thoughts and concentrating his contemplation on Amitābha Buddha in the Land of Utmost Bliss. Three times he saw the Three Saints of the West, and each time he remained calm and grave, speaking of it to no one.
In the twelfth year of the Yixi era of Emperor An of the Eastern Jin (

), on a night at the end of the seventh month, at the stupa east of the Prajna Terrace, Huiyuan was just rising from samadhi when he saw Amitābha Buddha, whose vast body filled all space. Within the pure encircling radiance were countless transformation Buddhas, while Avalokitesvara and Mahasthamaprapta stood attending on either side. He also saw the streams of light of the Land of Utmost Bliss, divided into fourteen branches, flowing up and down and proclaiming the Dharma-sounds of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and no-self. Amitābha Buddha told Huiyuan: "By the power of my original vow I come to comfort you. In seven days you shall be born in my land." He also saw Buddha-yasa, Hui Chi, Huiyong, Liu Yimin, and others of the Lotus Society who had already been reborn in the Western Pure Land, all standing beside Amitābha Buddha, who bowed to Huiyuan in greeting and asked: "Master, you were the first to set your mind on this; how is it that you have come so late

Huiyuan told his disciples Fajing and Huibao: "From the time I first came to Mount Lu to dwell in peace until now, in these eleven years I have seen the Three Saints of the West three times, and today I have seen them once again; my rebirth in the Pure Land is utterly certain
He then laid down his final instructions; on the sixth day of the eighth month he sat upright and entered quiescence, at the age of eighty-three.

blocks.text: Appendix: A Brief Life of Liu Yimin

inline.s: Liu Yimin (

), a famous lay Buddhist of the Jin dynasty, was named Chengzhi and styled Zhongsi, and was a native of Pengcheng (Tongshan county, Jiangsu). He lost his father young and served his mother with the utmost filial devotion. He was skilled in the doctrines of Laozi and Zhuangzi and did not carelessly mingle with the worldly men of his day. He first served the government as a military adviser, and though the princes and great ministers of the time recommended him one after another for higher office, Liu Chengzhi firmly declined them all.

At that time Master Huiyuan was living at Donglin Monastery on Mount Lu, cultivating the Buddha-recitation samadhi, and so Liu Chengzhi went there to take refuge with him. Master Huiyuan said: "Official rank brings great honor; why not accept it?" Liu Chengzhi replied: "The Jin dynasty has no firmness of bedrock, while sentient beings are in the peril of stacked eggs; why should I take office?" Later, because Liu Chengzhi would not bow to official rank, Emperor Liu Yu of the Liu-Song dynasty of the Southern Court gave him the name Yimin, "the one who has withdrawn from the world," in praise of his lofty virtue. At the same time a number of men of pure faith, such as Zong Que, Lei Cizong, Zhou Xuzhi, Zhang Ye, Zhang Quan, and Bi Yingzhi, also came to Mount Lu to practice under Master Huiyuan. Together they built dwellings before the images of the Three Saints of the West and founded the Lotus Society, cultivating the Pure Land Dharma gate in common, and Liu Yimin carved a vow in stone, which reads:

Once the principle of cause and condition, of change and transformation, is understood, the signs of coming and going, of birth and death, become plain. Once the rule that transmigration gives rise to rebirth accords with the facts, then the retribution of good and evil karma is a certainty. We know how hard it is to obtain a human body, and how swiftly it is lost, slipping away in a moment to sink into the six realms; we awaken to the impermanence of worldly things and the urgency with which birth and death press upon us. We understand that the evil retributions of the three evil paths press upon us in hot haste, and that the perilous evil destinies are hard to escape. This is why those worthy ones of one aspiration labored diligently at dawn and kept watchful at night, longing to look up for some rescue and deliverance!

As for what is called the inconceivable state, it can be reached only by sympathetic resonance, and cannot be pursued by form. If one can resonate with what truly exists, then even a distant road lies close at hand. If one seeks it where there is no real substance, then one wanders vast and vague with no goal at all. Today we are fortunate to have resonated with it without contriving it, to have set our hearts on the Western Pure Land, to set it forth in writing to declare our true faith, and to lay bare our feelings and vows between heaven and earth. And so these tokens of affinity communicated themselves in sleep and dream, until more than a hundred worthy ones came together to practice in common, a matter of heartfelt rejoicing. The assembled worthies gathered like clouds and gave forth light, their forms and shadows matching one another as though made by heaven and earth. Works and deeds can be harmonious only when there is a principle, and a thing so supreme as this cannot be accomplished by human effort alone. Truly it was heaven and earth setting in motion their sincerity and secretly assisting, that brought these worthies together in one place!

Yet the backgrounds and virtues of these people are uneven, and their good roots and merit are not the same. Though in the morning all alike seek the same goal of rebirth in the Pure Land, by evening their minds have shifted again; and this is so even among fellow practitioners of my own lineage, which is truly cause for sorrow. Therefore we rouse ourselves with deep feeling and bid the assembly straighten their robes and go to the hall of practice, so that all may bring one mind into play and entrust their hearts to the inconceivable ultimate (the Western Pure Land). We vow that all who practice together here may be reborn at ease in the Land of Utmost Bliss. And you who are outstanding and beyond compare, who are the first to be reborn in the Western Pure Land, do not roam at leisure alone in the towering clouds, forgetting to look after those still drowning in the deep valley.

Beholding the supremely wondrous heavenly countenance of Amitābha Buddha, our minds are opened and made to give rise to true illuminating awareness. The deluded false consciousness is awakened by the true mind, and the coarse heavy body is transformed into the supreme wondrous body born from a lotus. Leaning upon the lotus amid the waters of the eight good qualities, under the shade of the rows of seven-jeweled trees, we praise Amitābha Buddha. We fly through the vast space between heaven and earth, our garments drifting like clouds; we wander in the breeze scented with flowers and forget the years and months. Bowing our heads, we take leave of the three evil paths from afar; lifting our heads, we look proudly upon the heavenly palaces and take our eternal leave of the three realms. Drawing in living beings to continue the great path of rebirth in the Pure Land, gazing afar toward Amitābha Buddha, the Great Enlightened One, as our goal: if such an ideal can be reached, is it not grand and far-reaching indeed?

Liu Yimin later went north of the Xilin stream and built his own meditation hut, where he devoted himself to studying the profound principles of the Dharma, strictly observed the precepts, and composed poems on the Buddha-recitation samadhi. After living there half a year, in samadhi he saw Amitābha Buddha send forth light that illumined the earth, all of it turning golden. Fifteen years later, while he was reciting the Buddha's name, he saw Amitābha Buddha, whose white-curl light touched his body, and who let down his hand in comfort and welcome. Liu Yimin said: "How may I obtain the Tathagata's blessing of laying his hand upon my head and covering my body with his robe?" Hardly had he spoken when Amitābha Buddha stroked his head and draped a kashaya robe over him. On another day he dreamed that he entered the seven-jeweled lotus pond and saw blue and white lotuses, the water clear and still. Someone with a circular halo above his head and the swastika mark on his chest pointed to the pond water and said: "This is the water of the eight good qualities; you may drink it." Liu Yimin drank of it and found it surpassingly sweet. On waking, a rare fragrance issued from his pores. Then he said to those around him: "The conditions for my rebirth in the Pure Land have come!"

He then asked monks to recite the Lotus Sutra, nearly several hundred copies. Facing the Buddha image, Liu Yimin burned incense and bowed again and again, praying: "Through Śākyamuni Buddha's bequeathed teaching I have come to know of Amitābha Buddha in the Western Pure Land. This incense should first be offered to Śākyamuni Tathagata, next to Amitābha Buddha, and then to the Lotus Sutra; for it is by the merit of this sutra that I am able to attain rebirth in the Pure Land. I also vow that I and all sentient beings may be born together in the Western Pure Land." When he had finished speaking he bade farewell to the assembly, lay down on his bed, faced west with his palms joined, and passed away peacefully. This was in the sixth year of the Yixi era of Emperor An of the Eastern Jin (
), when he was fifty-nine years old.

Six years later, while Master Huiyuan sat in stillness in his retreat, in samadhi he saw Amitābha Buddha, whose body towered so greatly that it filled all space, with Avalokitesvara and Mahasthamaprapta attending at his left and right. Liu Yimin and those monks and lay members of the Lotus Society who had already been reborn stood before the Buddha, and, cupping their hands to Huiyuan, they said: "Master, you set your mind on this before we did; how is it that you have come so late?" Master Huiyuan passed into quiescence seven days later.

blocks.text: Appendix: Wang Qiaozhi's Poems on the Buddha-Recitation Samadhi

inline.s: No. 1
Here the wondrous working lies: to pass through being, gaze on the void. The spirit, through its darkness, clears; the senses, shining, grasp the coarse.
Gathering the subtle, the self is drawn on; the ground of every work is emptiness. Dissolve those three contemplations; forget this last remaining shred.
No. 2
In stillness without beginning, the principle is deep and threads the subtle. Melting, one forgets all comfort; then the numinous radiance opens wide.
The heart roams a distant realm; attainment comes without treading the trigger. Use it in emptiness; meet it in the rare.
No. 3
The spirit rests in heaven's stillness, mirroring round the morning clouds. With transformation it responds; with things it forms its kind.
It answers with no fixed direction; each receiver is distinguished by himself. Still as a mirror of the deep: golden water, the dust astir.
No. 4
I sigh over this one life, so long devoid of wisdom's sight. I lean upon the lofty and profound, and trust perhaps in hidden might.
Thoughts turn with the least exertion, deep beyond all fathoming. Most sublime is this one thought: fix the heart on the Western Ultimate.

Peng Shaosheng's Biographies of Lay Buddhists says: "Wang Qiaozhi was a man of Langya and served as governor of Linhe. Later he joined the White Lotus Society to serve Master Huiyuan, and with Liu Yimin and the other worthies composed Poems on the Buddha-Recitation Samadhi; Qiaozhi's poems alone have been handed down to the world."

Master Yinguang said: Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu, having received the Buddha's charge in a former life, returned by the power of his vow. Before he had read the Nirvāṇa Sutra, he wrote a treatise on the permanence of the Dharma-nature. Before he had seen the Avatamsaka Sutra, he expounded the doctrine that returns to the Pure Land. His teaching secretly accorded with the scriptures, and his way embraced all three capacities, high, middle, and low. It suited both principle and capacity, penetrating above and below. It fulfilled the Tathagata's original intent in appearing in the world and settled the great matter of living beings' birth and death. Had he not been a great bodhisattva manifesting himself, how could he have been so? Hence Master Kumarajiva said: "The scriptures say that in the East, in later times, there will be a Dharma-protecting bodhisattva who will greatly spread the Buddha-Dharma and the Pure Land Dharma gate." All the monks of the Western Regions declared that the land of Han possessed a Mahayana bodhisattva, and so they often bowed eastward and offered their hearts to Mount Lu. The traces of Master Huiyuan's spiritual principle cannot be measured. In the ninth year of the Taiyuan era, the jiashen year, of Emperor Xiaowu of the Eastern Jin (

), he first came to Mount Lu and stayed at Xilin Monastery, the monastery of his fellow disciple Master Huiyong. Later, as more and more people came to rely on him, Xilin Monastery was too small to hold them, and so Donglin Monastery was founded. When the planning began, the mountain spirit manifested its power and the timber came of itself. The governor Huan Yi then built it for him, and named its hall Shenyun, "Spirit-Transported," to make known the marvel. From then on more and more worthy monks and laymen came to follow him. In the fifteenth year of Taiyuan, the gengyin year (

), on the twenty-eighth day of the seventh month, he formed a society with one hundred and twenty-three monks and laymen to recite the Buddha's name and seek rebirth in the Western Pure Land. All of them, at the time of death, showed auspicious signs and were reborn there. This was because they possessed outstanding intelligence, and further received Master Huiyuan's guidance and the sharpening of one another among fellow practitioners, and so gained this benefit. These were the people of that first society. As for the Master's whole life, within more than thirty years, how could one ever count those who received the Dharma's transformation, cultivated pure karma, attained the Buddha-recitation samadhi, and ascended to the Land of Lotuses! (For the original text see Master Yinguang's Collected Writings
Preface to the Collected Writings of Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu, First Patriarch of the Lotus Lineage of the Jin Dynasty)

[The treatise on the permanence of the Dharma-nature] Master Huiyuan once wrote a Treatise on the Nature of Dharma to explain the principle that nirvāṇa is permanent. When Master Kumarajiva read it he praised it, saying: "Though the borderlands had not seen the definitive Mahayana scriptures, he has secretly accorded with the ultimate meaning of the Dharma." [Borderlands] refers to the Chinese lands of that time, for the Dharma had come but recently and many important scriptures had not yet been translated, especially the definitive Mahayana sutras. [He expounded the doctrine that returns to the Pure Land] In the Avatamsaka Sutra

Chapter on the Conduct and Vows of Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, the ten great kingly vows of Samantabhadra lead all back to the Pure Land, helping all living beings escape the sea of suffering of the Saha world and be reborn in the pure land of Amitābha Buddha in the Western Pure Land. Master Yinguang's words mean that although Master Huiyuan had not yet seen the Avatamsaka Sutra (it had not yet been translated at that time), he was already expounding the doctrine that returns to the Pure Land. [Western Regions] refers generally to the countries west of China, and specifically to India.
Master Huiyuan's influence on his own age and on later generations was exceedingly profound. Here are only a few examples (see Records of Pure Land Saints and Sages):
Eastern Jin
Sengji

Sengji entered Mount Lu to study the Dharma under Master Huiyuan, and he mastered and penetrated the essentials of the Buddha-Dharma. Just past the age of thirty, he came down the mountain into the city to take the teaching seat and expound the sutras, and he repeatedly served as the senior monk instructing the assembly. Master Huiyuan praised him, saying: "The one who can spread the Mahayana Dharma together with me must surely be you

Later, gravely ill, he earnestly and sincerely vowed to be reborn in the Pure Land and fixed his contemplation on the figure of Amitābha Buddha. Master Huiyuan gave Sengji a candle, saying: "You may concentrate your mind and recollect Amitābha Buddha and the Land of Utmost Bliss." Sengji then held the candle and leaned against the table, concentrating without the least distraction, and asked the assembled monks to recite the Immeasurable Life Sutra for him. At the fifth watch, Sengji handed the candle to his disciple Yuanbi and told him to hold the flame and walk in meditation with the assembly. Sengji himself lay down on his bed to rest awhile, and then dreamed that he was holding a candle and walking through the air; he saw Amitābha Buddha, who placed him in the palm of his hand and carried him throughout the ten directions. Then he suddenly awoke, and full of joy Sengji said: "In but a single night of contemplation and recollection I have received Amitābha Buddha's welcome. I have also come to understand that this physical body is only a false union of the four elements, and the feelings of sickness and pain have now entirely vanished." The next evening he suddenly rose to his feet, his gaze meeting the sky as though he saw something there, and he told his disciple Yuanbi: "The Buddha has come; I am going to be reborn

Then he turned to the west and passed away. It was the hottest part of summer, yet for three days his body showed no change, and a rare and heavy fragrance filled the air. He was forty-five years old.
Eastern Jin
Huigong, Sengguang, and Huilan

Huigong was a native of Fengcheng in Yuzhang, Jiangxi. He joined the Lotus Society on Mount Lu and, together with Sengguang, Huilan, and others, studied the Dharma under Master Huiyuan. Though Sengguang and the rest were not Huigong's equal in learning, they were more devout and earnest than he in concentrating their recollection on the Western Pure Land. Huilan once told Huigong: "Though you are tireless in study and vast in learning, do you not know what the scriptures say: 'It is like a deaf man playing music: he pleases others, but he himself does not hear it'?" When Huigong heard this he did not take it to heart and did not believe what Huilan said. In the seven years that followed, Huilan and the others passed away first, and at their deaths there were wondrous signs. Five years later, Huigong fell gravely and dangerously ill, and only then did he sigh and say: "Wandering and turning through the six realms, when will it ever stop? Between death and birth, coming and going, where shall I take my refuge

Then his tears fell like rain, and he bowed his head in prostration, vowing to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, his mind never wavering for an instant. One day he suddenly saw Amitābha Buddha come to welcome him with a golden lotus throne, and Huigong at once found himself seated upon it. He also saw Huilan and the others within the light upon the golden throne, who told Huigong: "Elder, you have been reborn in the Pure Land and already hold a place in the highest grade. We cannot contain our joy and gladness; we only regret that the conditions of the evil world of the five turbidities delayed you, so that we meet and lean upon one another only now, so late

That same day Huigong told the assembly of this wondrous sign, and then, joyful in heart and roused in spirit, he entered quiescence and was reborn. This was in the eleventh year of the Yixi era of Emperor An of the Eastern Jin (
Tang
Shandao
(Note: Shandao here is not Master Shandao, for his name is written with different characters. In Records of Pure Land Saints and Sages there is a separate entry, "Tang
Shandao (Second Patriarch of the Lotus Lineage)".)

Shandao was a native of Linzi (present-day Zibo, Shandong). He once entered the sutra library and, reaching out at random, took up the Contemplation Sutra of Immeasurable Life; thereafter he devoted himself single-mindedly to Buddha-recitation and cultivated the sixteen supreme contemplations of the Contemplation Sutra. Later he went to Mount Lu and visited the traces of Master Huiyuan's Lotus Society. He was moved to sorrow that he could not have met that gathering in person, and his longing for the Land of Utmost Bliss grew ever greater. Shandao then withdrew in seclusion to Mount Zhongnan, where he practiced the pratyutpanna-samadhi for several years. He personally beheld the seven-jeweled towers and the pure lotus ponds of the Land of Utmost Bliss, as clear and real as if he were there in person, as though before his very eyes. Later he went to Jinyang (present-day Taiyuan, Shanxi) and studied under Chan Master Daochuo, who taught him the Immeasurable Life Sutra.

Once Shandao prepared to enter samadhi for seven days, and Master Daochuo asked him to observe where he himself would be reborn in the next life. When he rose from samadhi, Shandao reported to Master Daochuo: "Master, you must repent of three offenses before you can be reborn in the Pure Land. You once placed a Buddha image beneath the window at the eaves while you yourself lived within a secure inner room; this is the first offense, and you should repent it before all the Buddhas. You also once put monks to labor and gave them orders; this is the second offense, and you should seek repentance before the monks of the four quarters. And in building dwellings you took the lives of many insects and ants; this is the third offense, and you should repent it before all living beings." When Master Daochuo heard this, he quietly reflected on his past faults, washed away the deluded mind of affliction and dust, and sincerely repented and asked forgiveness. Some time later, when Shandao again rose from samadhi, he told Master Daochuo: "Master, your offenses have been extinguished. When a white light comes to shine upon you, that will be the auspicious sign of your rebirth in the Pure Land."

Shandao spread the teaching in the capital, and those who came to take refuge and study under him were as numerous as a crowd in the marketplace. One day he suddenly fell slightly ill; he closed the door of his room and, within it, peacefully and quietly recited the Buddha's name and passed away. Then a rare fragrance and heavenly music drifted westward and gradually faded away.
Liu Song
Daobing (pronounced
bing

Daobing's secular surname was Chen, and he was a native of Yingchuan in Henan. He left home as a child and became a disciple of Master Huiyuan. Daobing was versed in both sutras and vinaya, and in daily life his words matched his deeds, his understanding and his practice according with each other; he applied his mind to investigating the Buddha-recitation samadhi, pressing on day and night without interruption. In the fourteenth year of the Yixi era of Emperor An of the Eastern Jin (

), the governor of Yuzhang, Wang Qian, came into the mountains to pay his respects, and asked Master Daobing to succeed Master Huiyuan in his seat. All the assembly looked up to him in their hearts for his virtue. In the twenty-second year of the Yuanjia era of Emperor Wen of the Liu-Song dynasty (
), he gathered the assembly to recite the Buddha's name, and then, seated in meditation, he passed away while reciting the Buddha's name, at the age of seventy-one.
Sui
Zhishun

Zhishun. His origins are not known. Because he admired the virtue and deeds of Great Master Huiyuan's past life, he entered Mount Lu and studied the Pure Land teaching. In the early years of the Daye era of the Sui emperor Yangdi (

), after he had finished lecturing on the Contemplation Sutra of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, he manifested illness. At the end of his life he saw parrots and peacocks, all of them mindful of the Buddha, mindful of the Dharma, mindful of the Sangha, and sounding subtle Dharma music. He then told his disciples: 'Today I am going to be reborn [in the Pure Land].' And thereupon he passed away and was reborn.
Ming
Deqing (Great Master Hanshan)
Deqing,

by imperial command regained the status of a monk, and on returning from retirement passed by Mount Lu, where he built a thatched hermitage beneath Five-Breast Peak. Following the example of Great Master Huiyuan, he observed the order of the six periods of the day and, with all the more diligence, cultivated the Pure Land teaching.
Song
Zhang Lun (
lun

Zhang Lun. His origins are not known. He rose to the office of Deputy Chief Controller of western Zhejiang. In ordinary times he devoutly cultivated the Pure Land teaching, and once requested Emperor Gaozong of the Southern Song to write the two characters 'Lotus Society' to hang at his gate. In this matter Zhang Lun presented a writing to the emperor, saying: 'Your servant has read the sutras of India and knows that beyond the world there is a land called the Land of Ultimate Bliss. In that land there is a Buddha named Amitābha. At first he enjoyed a land and dwelt in high royal estate. Later he abandoned the land and no longer dwelt upon the throne, transcended all in sovereign awakening, entered into his original mind, and realized the holy fruit. With the vast and deep power of his vows he universally ferries over the multitudes of living beings. His Land of Ultimate Bliss is adorned by the supreme and wondrous myriad precious things, and the ground is all paved with gold, with no peril of high mountains, rivers, hills, or deep valleys. The climate is fresh and pleasant as in spring throughout the year, without the unsettled changes of yin and yang, cold and heat, rain and shine. There is no suffering of hunger and cold, of age and sickness, of birth-and-death and the turning wheel; neither is there the turbid evil and unclean commingling of the five destinies. With these various supernormal powers Amitābha Buddha skillfully guides living beings, making them joyous and glad and so giving rise to faith. If only amid the daily and ordinary one can raise a single thought of a pure mind and recollect the holy name of Amitābha Buddha, then in that very present thought, pure and fully matured, perfect and complete, it merges with suchness and is of one Dharma-nature. When the illusory physical body is extinguished, this nature is not cut off, and in an instant the Buddha-land of Ultimate Bliss at once appears, as easy as taking up a contract and going to receive the thing one has left in keeping.'

Your servant reverently heard this teaching and therefore applied the more effort to cultivation, vigorous and untiring, without interruption. Thought after thought only the Buddha-name; in this manner I have practiced for several years already. All the members of my family, old and young, have without exception been transformed by it. Therefore on the east side of my old and humble house I dug a pond and planted lotus, imitating the manner of the Lotus Society that Great Master Huiyuan gathered, and each day I lead my wife and children in reciting the Buddha-name ten thousand times. In addition, in the last month of each spring and autumn, I choose an auspicious day and, at the Pujing Retreat, practice together with other good people of like faith. Those who hear of this and rejoice and join in gather like clouds and meet like rivers, and the sound of their chanting the Buddha-name is endless, like the surging tide of a great river.

Ever since Great Master Huiyuan founded the Lotus Society, several hundred years have now passed. During these years, whether monk or layman, those who have admired and longed for the high conduct he left behind, and who have esteemed and followed his lofty aspiration, have been no fewer in each generation. Yet most of them were hidden and unknown, silent as wood and stone. Why should your servant alone have the good fortune to receive from the Most High Emperor, Radiant Sage of Holy Longevity, the honors of his own imperial brush writing out the two large characters 'Lotus Society,' granting me a handwriting like clouds and beautiful jade? This is a privilege never before known. It makes the eyes of ten thousand people gaze upon it together, and the joy and delight of the multitude are hard to restrain. Not only is it displayed among the hundred officials, it is a splendid event rare even in a thousand years. And I sincerely pray that the world and the generations to come, whoever sees or hears of this, may all attain the Buddha-recitation samadhi and finally achieve the unexcelled bodhi. The benefit to living beings that this act of the emperor has conferred, how could it be measured by thought? Today your servant reverently records this matter upon metal and stone, in order to praise the emperor's great sage enterprise and reveal the auspicious mandate of the emperor's merit and fortune!

blocks.text: Biography of Great Master Huiyuan (Classical Chinese)

inline.s: Selected from the Records of the Pure Land Sages and Worthies
Jin
Huiyuan, the first patriarch of the Lotus (Pure Land) school.

Huiyuan was surnamed Jia and came from Loufan of Yanmen. As a child he loved learning, broadly mastered the Six Classics, and was especially skilled in Zhuangzi and Laozi. At that time the monk Daoan had founded a temple at the Hengshan of the Taihang range, and Huiyuan went to take refuge with him. Hearing Daoan expound the Prajna Sutra, he was suddenly and completely awakened, and so cast aside his hairpin and became his disciple. He pondered deeply and recited, continuing from night into day. Daoan sighed and said: 'The one who will make the Way flow on through the eastern land
(China)
, is it not Huiyuan!'
[Casting off the hairpin (
zan
)] Throwing away the hairpin used to secure the cap, a metaphor for abandoning office. [Receiving the study] Following a teacher in learning.

In the sixth year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin, passing through Xunyang, he saw Mount Lu, spacious and serene, fit for dwelling, and so established a Pure Retreat called Longquan Temple. At that time Huiyong, a fellow disciple of Huiyuan, was already residing in the West Grove of Mount Lu and wished to invite him to dwell together. But Huiyuan's companions in study and his gathered disciples were growing steadily more numerous,
(that is, Great Master Huiyuan's fellow practitioners and the disciples who took refuge with him became more and more numerous)
, and the West Grove was too cramped to house them. The Inspector Huan Yi, on Huiyuan's behalf, built another temple to the east of the mountain, and so it was called the East Grove.

Huiyuan thereupon led the assembly in the practice of the Way, dug a pond, and planted lotus. Upon the water he set a twelve-leaf lotus, which turned with the waves, marking off day and night, used as a measure for their practice of the Way. Soon pure and faithful persons from all quarters, having heard of his fame, came to him, one hundred twenty-three in number. Huiyuan said: 'In your coming here, can you have no thought for the Pure Land?' He then made images of the Three Sages of the West, instituted a pure fast, and established a society. He had Liu Yimin compose a vow text and had it engraved upon stone.

At that time several people such as Wang Qiaozhi also made verses on the Buddha-recitation samadhi to express their aims. Huiyuan wrote a preface for them, saying: 'Now what is the samadhi called? It is called single-minded contemplation and still thought. When thought is single, the will is unified and not divided; when thought is still, the qi is empty and the spirit clear. When qi is empty, wisdom is awake to its illumination; when the spirit is clear, there is no depth it does not penetrate. These two are the mysterious accord of nature, converging in one and producing their function. Moreover, the various samadhis are very many in name. Of those outstanding in merit and easily progressed in, the Buddha-recitation is foremost. Why? It exhausts the mystery and reaches the ultimate stillness, honored as the Tathagata. It embodies spirit and accords with transformation, responding without a fixed direction. And so one who enters this concentration becomes, in dark self-forgetfulness of knowing, taking his object and making it a mirror. The mirror being bright, inward illumination shines back and forth, and the myriad images arise within it. This is not what ears and eyes can reach
(or arrive at)

, yet hearing and seeing proceed within it. Then the spiritual marks are serene and one, pure and bright, natural of themselves; the primal sound knocks upon the heart, and the clinging feelings melt and brighten. Unless it be the supreme wonder of the world, who could attain anything like this! Therefore the worthy ones who uphold the Dharma all think upon the one covenant
kui

of the same principle. Moved by the passing of an inch of shade, and fearing that the store for the future is not yet accumulated, they wash their hearts in the Dharma hall and straighten their garments toward purity; the night deepens and they forget to sleep, rising early and diligent alone. They hope that the merit of earnest attainment may reach the aims of the three vehicles. Above, they aid the transcendent step with the rising of drawing up the white grass; below, they draw on the weak to advance and spur them on from behind. When one looks at the lines these various pieces have set flowing, is it only a matter of literary chanting?'
[One standard (
kui

)] The same principle. [Drawing up the white grass] That is, drawing up the white grass and it comes up together with its roots. Mao: the white grass, a kind of perennial grass; ru: the manner in which the roots of plants are linked together. A metaphor for mutual recommendation, where drawing in one person brings in many.
Because the scriptures of Jiangdong were largely lacking,
(the same as 'lacking')

Huiyuan sent his disciples far beyond the Congling range to purchase various Sanskrit texts and transmitted them to Guanzhong. All the sutras and vinayas that issued from Mount Lu numbered nearly a hundred juan. He also composed the Treatise on Dharma-nature to make clear the meaning of nirvāṇa
(nirvāṇa)
which is eternally abiding. Kumarajiva, when he saw it, sighed and said: 'Without having seen the great sutra of the frontier region, he already agrees with the principle in the dark.'

He dwelt on the mountain for thirty years, and his footprints never entered the profane world. He single-mindedly devoted himself to the Pure Land, purifying his mind in contemplation and visualization. Three times he saw the holy manifestation, yet, being deep and reticent, he did not speak of it. In the twelfth year of the Yixi era

on the evening of the last day of the seventh month, at the eastern chapel of the Prajna Terrace, as he was just rising from concentration, he saw Amitābha Buddha, whose body filled empty space. Amid the perfect halo were those whom the Buddha had emanated, with Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta attending on left and right. He also saw streams of water give forth light, parting into fourteen branches, flowing back and forth above and below, proclaiming the sound of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self. The Buddha said to Huiyuan: 'Because of the power of my primal vow, I have come to comfort you. Seven days from now you shall be born in my land.' He further saw those of the society who had already passed on, such as Buddhayashas, Huichi, Huiyong, and Liu Yimin, all at his side, who came forward and bowed, saying: 'Master, you aroused the mind long ago; why have you come so late?'

Huiyuan said to his disciples Fajing and Huibao: 'When I first dwelt here, within eleven years I three times saw the holy manifestation. Now I have seen it again, and my rebirth in the Pure Land is certain.' He then composed by himself his testamentary instruction. On the sixth day of the eighth month he entered the stillness while sitting upright, aged eighty-three.
